title: Comets: dirty snowballs with two tails
description: A comet is a lump of ice and dust left over from the birth of the solar system. When it swings near the Sun it grows not one tail but two — and they point in different directions.

body.heading: A snowball that boils in sunlight
paragraphs: Astronomer Fred Whipple called comets 'dirty snowballs': a nucleus of ice mixed with dark dust and rock, often only a few kilometres wide. Far from the Sun it is frozen and invisible; as it approaches, the ice turns straight to gas, jetting out and dragging dust with it to form a glowing head called the coma.
That outgassing is why comets brighten so unpredictably. A fresh crack in the crust can expose new ice and make a comet flare, while an old, crusted comet may disappoint.

body.heading: Two tails, two forces
paragraphs: The dust tail is broad, curved and yellowish — sunlight reflecting off grains pushed gently away from the Sun. The ion tail is narrow, straight and blue: gas charged by sunlight and swept directly outward by the solar wind, the stream of particles flowing from the Sun.
Because both tails are pushed away from the Sun, a comet leaving the inner solar system travels tail-first — the tails lead, the head follows.

takeaway: A comet is a dirty snowball of ice and dust that grows two tails near the Sun: a curved dust tail and a straight blue ion tail, both pointing away from the Sun.
